items.title: A finite cyclic group has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing its own
items.strategy: Let $G=\langle g\rangle$ have order $n$. For a positive divisor $d$ of $n$ show $\langle g^{n/d}\rangle$ has order $d$ by computing the order of $g^{n/d}$. For uniqueness, let $H\le G$ with $|H|=d$; every $h\in H$ satisfies $h^d=e$ by Lagrange, and the elements of $G$ with $x^d=e$ are exactly the $n/d$-th powers, of which there are $d$, so $H=\langle g^{n/d}\rangle$. Finally $\langle g^{n/d}\rangle\subseteq\langle g^{n/e}\rangle$ exactly when $d\mid e$. Take $n\ge1$ so the trivial group ($d=1$) is covered.

items.title: A cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly $\varphi(n)$ generators
items.strategy: Transport along an isomorphism with $(\mathbb Z/n,+)$: the class $[a]_n$ generates $\mathbb Z/n$ exactly when $[a]_n$ is a unit, which is the coprimality criterion, and the units are counted by $\varphi(n)$. Check $n=1$, where the single element is a generator and $\varphi(1)=1$.

items.title: The relative Frobenius $x\mapsto x^q$ of an extension of finite fields
The elements of a finite extension fixed by the $q$-power map are exactly the base field
items.strategy: Every $a$ in the base field of order $q$ satisfies $a^q=a$, so the base field is contained in the fixed set. Conversely the fixed set is the root set of $t^q-t$, which has at most $q$ roots in the extension by the root bound, and the base field already supplies $q$ of them.

items.title: For a degree-$n$ extension of a field of order $q$, the $q$-power map has order exactly $n$
items.strategy: The tower law over the prime field gives $|E|=q^n$. Then $x^{q^n}=x$ on $E$, so the $n$-th iterate is the identity. If the $m$-th iterate were the identity for some $1\le m<n$, all $q^n$ elements of $E$ would be roots of $t^{q^m}-t$, contradicting the root bound since $q^m<q^n$. Include $n=1$, where the map is the identity and has order one.

items.title: A finite extension of a finite field of order $q$ is Galois with cyclic Galois group generated by $x\mapsto x^q$
items.strategy: Let $E/\mathbb F_q$ have degree $n$ and let $G=\langle\varphi_q\rangle$, of order $n$. Artin's fixed-field theorem gives $[E:E^{G}]=|G|=n$ and $\operatorname{Aut}(E/E^{G})=G$; the fixed field is $\mathbb F_q$, so $\operatorname{Aut}(E/\mathbb F_q)=G$ has order $n=[E:\mathbb F_q]$, which is the Galois criterion. No separate separability or normality argument is needed once Artin's theorem is applied to $G$.

items.title: The intermediate fields of $\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q$ are the $\mathbb F_{q^d}$, one for each positive divisor $d$ of $n$
items.strategy: Read the correspondence off a cyclic group. The subgroups of $\langle\varphi_q\rangle$ are the $\langle\varphi_q^{d}\rangle$ for $d\mid n$, exactly one of each order $n/d$. The fixed field of $\langle\varphi_q^{d}\rangle$ is $\{x: x^{q^{d}}=x\}$ directly from the definition of a fixed field, and the fundamental theorem gives $[\mathbb F_{q^{n}}:K^{\langle\varphi_q^{d}\rangle}]=n/d$, hence degree $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$ and order $q^{d}$; the fixed-field lemma is the case $d=1$, which is what identifies the bottom of the lattice as $\mathbb F_q$ rather than something larger. Inclusion between two of them corresponds to reverse inclusion of subgroups, which is divisibility of the degrees.

items.title: The Galois description of the subfields of a finite field and the elementary divisibility criterion agree
A monic irreducible of degree $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$ has the $d$ distinct roots $\alpha,\alpha^{q},\dots,\alpha^{q^{d-1}}$
items.strategy: Let $\alpha$ be a root of $\pi$ in an extension. Then $\mathbb F_q(\alpha)$ has degree $d$, so it is $\mathbb F_{q^{d}}$ and is Galois over $\mathbb F_q$ with group generated by $\varphi_q$. Each $\varphi_q^{i}(\alpha)=\alpha^{q^{i}}$ is again a root of $\pi$. If two of $\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{q^{d-1}}$ coincided, $\alpha$ would satisfy $x^{q^{j}}=x$ for some $0<j<d$ and hence lie in a proper subfield, contradicting $\mathbb F_q(\alpha)=\mathbb F_{q^{d}}$. The factor theorem then makes $\prod_{i<d}(t-\alpha^{q^{i}})$ a monic degree-$d$ divisor of $\pi$, so equal to it.

items.title: $\sum_{d\mid n}d\,N_q(d)=q^{n}$ for the counts $N_q(d)$ of monic irreducibles of degree $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$
items.strategy: The published factorisation of $t^{q^{n}}-t$ groups its monic irreducible factors by degree; each degree-$d$ factor contributes $d$ to the total degree and each occurs exactly once. Comparing degrees on the two sides gives the identity. Record that $N_q(d)$ is finite because there are only $q^{d}$ monic polynomials of degree $d$, and check $n=1$, where the identity reads $N_q(1)=q$.

items.title: Normal bases of a finite Galois extension
A polynomial vanishing at every tuple from an infinite subdomain is the zero polynomial
items.strategy: Induct on the number of indeterminates. For one indeterminate a nonzero polynomial of degree $m$ has at most $m$ roots in the ambient domain, while the infinite subdomain supplies more than $m$ elements. For $m>1$ write $f$ as a polynomial in the last indeterminate with coefficients in the polynomial ring on the others; each coefficient then vanishes on every tuple, so is zero by the inductive hypothesis. State it as $R\subseteq S$ with $R$ infinite and $f\in S[x_1,\dots,x_m]$, which is the form the normal basis argument uses with $R=F$ and $S=K$.

items.title: For a finite Galois extension, $(\alpha_j)$ is a base-field basis exactly when the matrix $(\sigma_i\alpha_j)$ is invertible
items.strategy: If the $\alpha_j$ are dependent over $F$, say $\sum_j a_j\alpha_j=0$ with $a_j\in F$ not all zero, then applying each $\sigma_i$ gives $A a=0$ with $a\neq0$, so $A$ is not invertible. Conversely, if the $\alpha_j$ are a basis and $\sum_i c_i\sigma_i(\alpha_j)=0$ for all $j$ with $c_i\in K$, then $F$-linearity of each $\sigma_i$ spreads the relation to all of $K$, so Dedekind independence forces $c=0$; hence $x\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}x$ is injective, so an isomorphism by rank-nullity, so $\det A^{\mathsf T}=\det A$ is a unit and $A$ is invertible.

items.title: Over an infinite base field, no nonzero polynomial vanishes at the conjugate tuple of every element
items.strategy: Fix a base-field basis $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ of $K$ and let $A=(\sigma_i\alpha_j)$, invertible by the preceding lemma. Writing a general $\alpha=\sum_j c_j\alpha_j$ with $c_j\in F$ gives the conjugate tuple $Ac$. If $f$ vanished at every conjugate tuple, the polynomial $g(x)=f(Ax)$ would vanish at every $c\in F^{n}$, so $g=0$ by the several-variable vanishing lemma; substituting $A^{-1}$ recovers $f=0$.

items.title: Every finite Galois extension of an infinite field has a normal basis
items.strategy: Number the group as $\sigma_1=\mathrm{id},\dots,\sigma_n$ and let $B$ be the matrix of indeterminates with $B_{ij}=x_k$ when $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_k$. Setting $x_1=1$ and the other indeterminates to $0$ turns $B$ into a permutation matrix, whose transpose is its inverse, so its determinant is a unit; hence $\det B$ is a nonzero polynomial. Algebraic independence supplies $\alpha$ with $\det(\sigma_i\sigma_j\alpha)\neq0$, and the conjugate-matrix criterion applied to $\alpha_j=\sigma_j\alpha$ makes $\{\sigma\alpha\}$ a basis.

items.title: Every finite cyclic extension has a normal basis
items.strategy: View $K$ as an $F$-vector space of dimension $n$ and $\sigma$, a generator of the group, as an $F$-linear endomorphism. Then $\sigma^{n}=\mathrm{id}$, so the minimal polynomial divides $x^{n}-1$; Dedekind independence makes $\mathrm{id},\sigma,\dots,\sigma^{n-1}$ linearly independent over $F$ as maps, so the minimal polynomial has degree at least $n$ and therefore equals $x^{n}-1$. The characteristic polynomial is monic of degree $n$ and is divisible by the minimal polynomial, so the two agree and a cyclic vector $\alpha$ exists; its power basis under $\sigma$ is exactly the conjugate family $\{\sigma^{i}\alpha\}$.

items.title: Every finite Galois extension has a normal basis
items.strategy: Split on the base field. If $F$ is infinite, apply the infinite-base-field theorem. If $F$ is finite, then $K$ is a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space over a finite field and so is itself finite, and the Frobenius theorem makes $K/F$ cyclic, so the cyclic case applies. The two cases are exhaustive, which is the whole content of the split.

items.title: The group $\mu_n(K)$ of $n$-th roots of unity in a field, and primitive $n$-th roots of unity
$\mu_n(K)$ is cyclic of order dividing $n$, and has a primitive $n$-th root of unity exactly when its order is $n$
items.strategy: The set $\mu_n(K)$ is a subgroup of $K^\times$, finite because its elements are roots of $t^{n}-1$ and a field is a domain, hence cyclic by the published subgroup theorem. Its order divides $n$ because every element has order dividing $n$ and the group is cyclic. A generator has order equal to the group order, so a primitive $n$-th root of unity exists exactly when that order is $n$, and there are then $\varphi(n)$ of them.

items.title: $t^{n}-1$ is separable over $K$ exactly when the characteristic does not divide $n$, and then a splitting field carries $n$ distinct $n$-th roots of unity
items.strategy: The derivative of $t^{n}-1$ is $n t^{n-1}$, whose only root is $0$ when $n\neq0$ in $K$ and which is the zero polynomial otherwise; the gcd criterion turns this into separability exactly when the characteristic does not divide $n$. Under that hypothesis a splitting field has $n$ distinct roots, so $\mu_n$ there is cyclic of order $n$ with $\varphi(n)$ generators, and adjoining any one of them gives the whole splitting field since every root is a power of it. Cover $n=1$, where the polynomial is $t-1$.

items.title: In characteristic $p$ the only $p^{k}$-th root of unity is $1$, and $t^{p^{k}}-1=(t-1)^{p^{k}}$
items.strategy: Iterating the freshman's dream in $K[t]$ gives $(t-1)^{p^{k}}=t^{p^{k}}-1$, so the only root is $1$. Deduce that for $n=p^{k}m$ with $p\nmid m$ one has $\mu_n(K)=\mu_m(K)$, which is why every later statement about $\mu_n$ carries the hypothesis that the characteristic does not divide $n$ rather than losing generality.

items.title: The cyclotomic extension $K(\mu_n)$ as a splitting field of $t^{n}-1$
$K(\mu_n)/K$ is Galois and $\sigma\mapsto a_\sigma$ embeds its Galois group into $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$
items.strategy: Galois because a splitting field of a separable polynomial. An automorphism carries a primitive $n$-th root $\zeta$ to a primitive $n$-th root, hence to $\zeta^{a}$ with $a$ coprime to $n$, and the exponent is well defined modulo $n$ because $\zeta$ has order $n$. Multiplicativity of exponents makes $\sigma\mapsto[a_\sigma]$ a homomorphism, and it is injective because $\zeta$ generates the extension. Check independence of the chosen primitive root by writing any other root of unity as a power of $\zeta$.

items.title: The Galois group of a cyclotomic extension is abelian
items.strategy: A subgroup of an abelian group is abelian, and multiplication on $\mathbb Z/n$ is commutative, so the embedded image and hence the Galois group is abelian.

items.title: For $\gcd(n,q)=1$ the image of $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb F_q(\mu_n)/\mathbb F_q)$ in $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ is generated by $[q]$
items.strategy: The extension $\mathbb F_q(\mu_n)/\mathbb F_q$ is an extension of finite fields, so its Galois group is generated by $\varphi_q$, whose effect on a primitive $n$-th root of unity is $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{q}$. Hence the embedded image is $\langle[q]\rangle$, and the degree, being the order of the group, is the multiplicative order of $[q]$ modulo $n$. Note the hypothesis $\gcd(n,q)=1$ is what makes $[q]$ a unit.

items.title: The cyclotomic polynomials $\Phi_n\in\mathbb Z[t]$, defined by $\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d=t^{n}-1$
The recursion defines a unique monic $\Phi_n\in\mathbb Z[t]$, of degree $\varphi(n)$
items.strategy: Strong induction on $n$. The product of the $\Phi_d$ for proper divisors $d$ is monic with integer coefficients, so dividing $t^{n}-1$ by it is division by a monic polynomial over $\mathbb Z$, which has a unique quotient and remainder there; the remainder is zero because the division is already exact over $\mathbb Q$ and uniqueness transfers. The degree is $n-\sum_{d\mid n,\,d<n}\varphi(d)=\varphi(n)$ by the published divisor-sum identity for the totient. This is the well-definedness obligation of the definition and must be a numbered item, not a parenthesis: the division is over $\mathbb Z$, not over a field.

items.title: $\Phi_1(0)=-1$ and $\Phi_n(0)=1$ for $n\ge2$
items.strategy: Evaluate $\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d=t^{n}-1$ at $t=0$: the right side is $-1$ and $\Phi_1(0)=-1$, so the product of $\Phi_d(0)$ over divisors $d>1$ is $1$. Strong induction gives $\Phi_d(0)=1$ for $1<d<n$, leaving $\Phi_n(0)=1$. Handle $n=2$ as the first case beyond the base.

items.title: Over a field whose characteristic does not divide $n$, the roots of $\Phi_n$ are exactly the primitive $n$-th roots of unity
items.strategy: Reduce the integer polynomial into $K$ and work in a splitting field of $t^{n}-1$, where that polynomial is separable. Strong induction on $n$: a root $\alpha$ of $\Phi_n$ has $\alpha^{n}=1$, and if its order were a proper divisor $d$ of $n$ it would be a root of $\Phi_d$ as well, making it a repeated root of $t^{n}-1$. Counting degrees, $\Phi_n$ has $\varphi(n)$ roots and there are $\varphi(n)$ primitive $n$-th roots of unity, so the two sets coincide and $\Phi_n$ is separable.

items.title: $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over $K$ exactly when $[K(\zeta_n):K]=\varphi(n)$, exactly when the embedding into $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ is onto
items.strategy: A primitive $n$-th root $\zeta$ is a root of $\Phi_n$, so its minimal polynomial over $K$ divides $\Phi_n$; equality holds exactly when the degrees agree, that is when $[K(\zeta):K]=\varphi(n)$, and since $K(\zeta)=K(\mu_n)$ that is exactly when the injection into a group of order $\varphi(n)$ is surjective.

items.title: $\Phi_{p^{r}}(t)=\sum_{k<p}t^{kp^{r-1}}$, and $\Phi_{p^{r}}(t+1)$ is Eisenstein at $p$
items.strategy: The recursion at $n=p^{r}$ telescopes to $\Phi_{p^{r}}(t)=(t^{p^{r}}-1)/(t^{p^{r-1}}-1)$, which is the displayed sum. Its value at $t=1$ is $p$, giving the constant term of the translate; modulo $p$ the numerator and denominator are $(t-1)^{p^{r}}$ and $(t-1)^{p^{r-1}}$, so the reduction of the translate is $t^{p^{r}-p^{r-1}}$ and every non-leading coefficient is divisible by $p$. Eisenstein then gives irreducibility of the translate, and translation by $1$ is a ring automorphism of $\mathbb Q[t]$, so $\Phi_{p^{r}}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. This is a self-contained route for prime powers, independent of the general argument that follows.

items.title: If $p$ is a prime not dividing $n$, a rational minimal polynomial of a primitive $n$-th root of unity also kills its $p$-th power
items.strategy: Write $\Phi_n=fg$ with $f$ the minimal polynomial of $\zeta$; both are monic factors of a monic integer polynomial, so both lie in $\mathbb Z[t]$ by Gauss's lemma. If $g(\zeta^{p})=0$ then $f$ and $g(t^{p})$ share the root $\zeta$, hence a nonconstant common factor over $\mathbb Q$ by gcd stability, hence over $\mathbb Z$. Reducing modulo $p$ and using $\overline g(t^{p})=\overline g(t)^{p}$ gives $\overline f$ and $\overline g$ a common nonconstant factor, so $t^{n}-1$ has a repeated root modulo $p$ — impossible since $p\nmid n$ makes it separable there. Record where $p\nmid n$ is used; without it the last step fails.

items.title: $\Phi_n$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[t]$ for every $n\ge1$
items.strategy: Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ of one primitive $n$-th root $\zeta$. Every other primitive $n$-th root is $\zeta^{a}$ with $a$ coprime to $n$, and such an $a$ is a product of primes none of which divides $n$; applying the preceding lemma once per prime factor shows $f$ vanishes at every primitive $n$-th root. So $f$ has at least $\varphi(n)$ roots and divides $\Phi_n$, which has degree $\varphi(n)$, forcing $f=\Phi_n$.

items.title: $[\mathbb Q(\zeta_n):\mathbb Q]=\varphi(n)$ and $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_n)/\mathbb Q)\cong(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$
items.strategy: Combine irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$ with the general criterion: irreducibility of $\Phi_n$ is exactly surjectivity of the embedding, so the injection is an isomorphism and the degree is the order $\varphi(n)$ of the target.

items.title: For $\gcd(n,q)=1$ the reduction of $\Phi_n$ in $\mathbb F_q[t]$ is a product of distinct monic irreducibles, each of degree the order of $[q]$ modulo $n$
items.strategy: The reduction is separable because it divides $t^{n}-1$, which is separable when $\gcd(n,q)=1$. Every root is a primitive $n$-th root of unity, and adjoining one gives $\mathbb F_q(\mu_n)$, whose degree over $\mathbb F_q$ is the order of $[q]$ modulo $n$; the degree of the irreducible factor with that root is that same degree. So every irreducible factor has the same degree, and distinctness is separability.

items.title: The reduction of $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over $\mathbb F_q$ exactly when $[q]$ generates $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$
items.strategy: Irreducibility means one factor, so the common factor degree equals $\deg\Phi_n=\varphi(n)$, that is the order of $[q]$ is the order of the whole group. In particular this can happen only when $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ is cyclic.

items.title: For $E/F$ finite Galois and $L/F$ finite inside a common field, $[EL:F]=[E:F][L:F]/[E\cap L:F]$
items.strategy: The translation theorem gives $\operatorname{Gal}(EL/L)\cong\operatorname{Gal}(E/E\cap L)$, so $[EL:L]=[E:E\cap L]$, which the tower law rewrites as $[E:F]/[E\cap L:F]$. Multiplying by $[L:F]$ through the tower $F\subseteq L\subseteq EL$ gives the formula. Note the hypothesis that one of the two is Galois is genuinely needed and record it.

items.title: $K(\mu_m)K(\mu_n)=K(\mu_{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)})$
items.strategy: Both $\mu_m$ and $\mu_n$ sit inside $\mu_{\ell}$ for $\ell=\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)$, so the compositum is contained in $K(\mu_\ell)$. Conversely the subgroup of the cyclic group $\mu_\ell$ generated by a primitive $m$-th and a primitive $n$-th root has order divisible by both $m$ and $n$, hence by $\ell$, so it is all of $\mu_\ell$. Require the characteristic to divide neither $m$ nor $n$ and say so in the statement.

items.title: $\varphi(m)\varphi(n)=\varphi(\gcd(m,n))\,\varphi(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n))$
items.strategy: Compare the two sides prime by prime using the product formula: for each prime $p$, the exponents in $m$ and $n$ are $a$ and $b$, and the exponents in the gcd and lcm are $\min(a,b)$ and $\max(a,b)$, whose multiset is $\{a,b\}$. Treat the case $p\nmid mn$ and the case where exactly one of $a,b$ is zero explicitly.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\mu_m)\cap\mathbb Q(\mu_n)=\mathbb Q(\mu_{\gcd(m,n)})$
items.strategy: One inclusion is immediate from $\mathbb Q(\mu_d)\subseteq\mathbb Q(\mu_m)$ for $d\mid m$. For equality compare degrees: the compositum is $\mathbb Q(\mu_{\operatorname{lcm}})$, so the compositum degree formula gives $[\mathbb Q(\mu_m)\cap\mathbb Q(\mu_n):\mathbb Q]=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)/\varphi(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n))$, which the totient identity turns into $\varphi(\gcd(m,n))$. State this for $\mathbb Q$ only: the same equality is false over a general base field.

items.title: For an odd prime $p$, $\mathbb Q(\zeta_p)$ has exactly one intermediate field of degree two over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: The Galois group is $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, the unit group of a field, hence cyclic, of order $p-1$, which is even for odd $p$. A finite cyclic group of even order has exactly one subgroup of index two, and the correspondence turns that into exactly one intermediate field of degree two. A Remark records that identifying that field concretely is a separate computation this proof does not carry out.

items.title: For every $n\ge1$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ with $p\equiv1\pmod n$
items.strategy: Take $n\ge2$ and a finite set $S$ of such primes with product $q$. For large $k$ the integer $N=\Phi_n(knq)$ exceeds $1$; since $\Phi_n(0)=1$, every prime dividing $knq$ leaves $N\equiv1$, so a prime divisor $p$ of $N$ divides neither $k$, nor $n$, nor $q$. As $p\nmid n$, the class of $knq$ in $\mathbb F_p$ is a root of $\Phi_n$, hence a primitive $n$-th root of unity there, so $n$ divides $p-1$ by Lagrange. That produces a prime outside $S$. Handle $n=1$ separately, where the claim is that there are infinitely many primes.

items.title: Every finite abelian group is a quotient of $(\mathbb Z/n)^{k}$ for some $n$ and $k$
items.strategy: Write the group in invariant-factor form as a product of $k$ cyclic groups of orders $d_1\mid\cdots\mid d_k$ and put $n=d_k$. Each $\mathbb Z/n$ surjects onto $\mathbb Z/d_i$ because $d_i\mid n$, and the product of these surjections is a surjection from $(\mathbb Z/n)^{k}$. Cover the trivial group.

items.title: Every finite abelian group is the Galois group of some finite Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Reduce to $G=(\mathbb Z/n)^{k}$ by the preceding lemma, since a quotient of a Galois group over $\mathbb Q$ is again one by the normal-subgroup clause. Choose distinct primes $p_1,\dots,p_k$ each congruent to $1$ modulo $n$; each $(\mathbb Z/p_i)^\times$ is cyclic of order $p_i-1$, so it surjects onto $\mathbb Z/n$. The Chinese remainder theorem identifies $(\mathbb Z/p_1\cdots p_k)^\times$ with the product of the $(\mathbb Z/p_i)^\times$, giving a surjection from $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_{p_1\cdots p_k})/\mathbb Q)$ onto $G$; its kernel corresponds to an intermediate field with the required group.

items.title: Every intermediate field of $\mathbb Q(\mu_n)/\mathbb Q$ is Galois over $\mathbb Q$ with abelian Galois group
items.strategy: Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, so every intermediate field is Galois over $\mathbb Q$, and its group is a quotient of an abelian group, hence abelian.

items.title: Recorded, not proved: every finite abelian extension of $\mathbb Q$ lies in a cyclotomic field

title: Finite Fields and Cyclotomic Extensions — Examples

items.title: $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb F_8/\mathbb F_2)$ is cyclic of order three with no proper intermediate field
items.strategy: Work in the published presentation $\mathbb F_8=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^{3}+t+1)$ and tabulate the squaring map on all eight elements. Its orbits on the six elements outside $\mathbb F_2$ are two triples, the group is generated by squaring and has order three, and since three is prime the only divisors are one and three, so there is no proper intermediate field.

items.title: The intermediate fields of $\mathbb F_{2^{12}}/\mathbb F_2$ match the divisors of twelve
items.strategy: List the six positive divisors of twelve and the corresponding subfields, drawing the containments and checking them against divisibility; contrast $\mathbb F_{2^{4}}$ and $\mathbb F_{2^{6}}$, neither containing the other, whose intersection is $\mathbb F_{2^{2}}$ and whose compositum is $\mathbb F_{2^{12}}$.

items.title: The divisor-sum identity at $q=2$, $n=3$ finds exactly two monic irreducible cubics
items.strategy: The identity reads $N_2(1)+3N_2(3)=8$ with $N_2(1)=2$, so $N_2(3)=2$; exhibit $t^{3}+t+1$ and $t^{3}+t^{2}+1$ and confirm by the root test that the remaining monic cubics all have a root in $\mathbb F_2$.

items.title: The four roots of $t^{4}+t+1$ over $\mathbb F_2$ are the Frobenius powers of any one of them
items.strategy: Take $\alpha$ with $\alpha^{4}=\alpha+1$ and compute $\alpha^{2},\alpha^{4},\alpha^{8}$ in the basis $1,\alpha,\alpha^{2},\alpha^{3}$, checking each is a root and that $\alpha^{16}=\alpha$ closes the orbit at length four.

items.title: A normal basis of $\mathbb F_8$ over $\mathbb F_2$
items.strategy: With $\mathbb F_8=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^{3}+t+1)$ and $\alpha$ the class of $t$, compute $\alpha,\alpha^{2},\alpha^{4}$ in the power basis and check the resulting three-by-three matrix over $\mathbb F_2$ is invertible, so the three conjugates form a normal basis.

items.title: $\{1+i,\,1-i\}$ is a normal basis of $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ while $\{1,i\}$ is not
items.strategy: The nontrivial automorphism is conjugation. The conjugates of $1+i$ are $1+i$ and $1-i$, whose conjugate matrix has determinant $-2i\neq0$. By contrast $\{1,i\}$ is a basis but its two members are not in one orbit, and the orbit $\{i,-i\}$ of $i$ is not a basis; both failures are worth stating because they separate the two conditions in the definition.

items.title: FALSE: every basis of a finite field over a subfield is a normal basis
items.strategy: Refute in $\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^{2}+t+1)$: the pair $\{1,\alpha\}$ is a basis over $\mathbb F_2$, but the only automorphism orbits are $\{1\}$ and $\{\alpha,\alpha+1\}$, and neither orbit is $\{1,\alpha\}$. The normal basis theorem asserts the existence of one such basis, never that every basis is one.

items.title: $\Phi_1$ through $\Phi_{12}$ computed from the divisor recursion
items.strategy: Run the recursion in order, dividing $t^{n}-1$ by the product of the earlier $\Phi_d$ over $\mathbb Z$, and tabulate the results with their degrees against $\varphi(n)$. Note that every division is exact and stays in $\mathbb Z[t]$, which is the content of the well-definedness theorem.

items.title: $\Phi_7(t+1)$ is Eisenstein at seven
items.strategy: Expand $((t+1)^{7}-1)/t$ by the binomial theorem, exhibit the coefficients $7,21,35,35,21,7$ and the constant term $7$, and check the three Eisenstein conditions at the prime seven, concluding irreducibility of $\Phi_7$ over $\mathbb Q$.

items.title: $\Phi_5$ has four roots in $\mathbb F_{11}$
items.strategy: Since $11\equiv1\pmod 5$, the order of $[11]$ modulo five is one, so every irreducible factor is linear; verify by exhibiting the factorisation of $t^{4}+t^{3}+t^{2}+t+1$ over $\mathbb F_{11}$ and checking each root has multiplicative order five.

items.title: $\Phi_7$ factors over $\mathbb F_2$ into the two monic irreducible cubics
items.strategy: The order of $[2]$ modulo seven is three, so both factors are cubic; multiply out $(t^{3}+t+1)(t^{3}+t^{2}+1)$ over $\mathbb F_2$ to confirm, and identify the two Frobenius orbits $\{\zeta,\zeta^{2},\zeta^{4}\}$ and $\{\zeta^{3},\zeta^{6},\zeta^{5}\}$ of primitive seventh roots of unity.

items.title: $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12})/\mathbb Q)\cong(\mathbb Z/12)^\times$ and its three quadratic subfields
items.strategy: List $(\mathbb Z/12)^\times=\{1,5,7,11\}$, check every element squares to the identity, and name its three subgroups of order two. Match each fixed field to $\mathbb Q(i)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ by exhibiting an element of $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12})$ fixed by the corresponding subgroup and squaring to $-1$, $3$ and $-3$ respectively.

items.title: In characteristic three, $t^{3}-1=(t-1)^{3}$ and $\mu_6$ coincides with $\mu_2$
items.strategy: Expand $(t-1)^{3}$ over $\mathbb F_3$ to see the middle coefficients vanish, so the only cube root of unity is one; then $\mu_6=\mu_2=\{1,-1\}$ in every field of characteristic three, and $t^{6}-1$ has two distinct roots rather than six.

items.title: $\mathbb F_3(\mu_5)\cap\mathbb F_3(\mu_7)$ is larger than $\mathbb F_3$ although five and seven are coprime
items.strategy: Compute the order of $[3]$ modulo five as four and modulo seven as six, so the two extensions are $\mathbb F_{3^{4}}$ and $\mathbb F_{3^{6}}$, whose intersection is $\mathbb F_{3^{2}}$ by the subfield lattice. This is the witness that the rational intersection theorem is a statement about $\mathbb Q$ and not a general fact.

items.title: FALSE: every cyclotomic polynomial has all coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$
items.strategy: The claim survives every $n$ below $105$, which is exactly what makes it worth stating. Refute it by computing $\Phi_{105}$ from the recursion and exhibiting the coefficient $-2$ that it carries; report the exact monomials at which that coefficient occurs.

items.title: FALSE: $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over every field
items.strategy: Refute with the reduction of $\Phi_5$ over $\mathbb F_{11}$, which is a product of four linear factors. Say precisely what the irreducibility theorem does claim: it is a statement about the base field $\mathbb Q$, and the finite-field factorisation theorem is what governs the general case.

items.title: FALSE: $\mu_n(K)$ has $n$ elements in every field $K$
items.strategy: Two independent refutations: in $\mathbb Q$ the group $\mu_3$ is trivial because $t^{3}-1$ has one rational root, and in characteristic three $\mu_3$ is trivial for a different reason, namely inseparability. State both, since the two failures have different causes and only the second is repaired by passing to a splitting field.

items.title: FALSE: every finite abelian group is $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_n)/\mathbb Q)$ for some $n$
items.strategy: For $n\ge3$ the class of $-1$ is a unit of order two, so $\varphi(n)$ is even by Lagrange, and $\varphi(1)=\varphi(2)=1$; hence no cyclotomic field over $\mathbb Q$ has Galois group of order three. Contrast with the theorem actually proved, which produces a subfield of a cyclotomic field, not the cyclotomic field itself.

items.title: A degree-three Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$ inside $\mathbb Q(\zeta_7)$
items.strategy: Since $(\mathbb Z/7)^\times$ is cyclic of order six, it has a unique subgroup of order two, generated by $[-1]$; its fixed field is $\mathbb Q(\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1})$, of degree three over $\mathbb Q$ and Galois with cyclic group of order three. Exhibit the minimal polynomial $t^{3}+t^{2}-2t-1$ of that generator and verify it by expanding the power sums of $\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1}$.
